prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The five frames show a close dining-table scene: the tabletop and seated people occupy roughly 0.4–1.5 m in front of the camera wearer, while the darker upper background is approximately 2 m or more away. Bright foreground arms and hands—especially at the lower left in frame 1, lower centre in frames 2–3, and centre-right in frame 4—appear within about 0.2–0.7 m; plates, cups, utensils, and papers lie slightly farther away on the table, roughly 0.5–1.2 m. Across the strip, nearby arms shift laterally and upward, while the seated figures remain at broadly similar depths, indicating camera turning and limb movement rather than a clear approach or retreat. The depth map makes near-arm versus far-table/background layering clearer than the dark RGB, but its smooth, relative shading, merged boundaries, and very bright limbs make metre estimates and distances between overlapping people unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates a dining table, people, cups, a bowl, a fork, and a knife, revealing object boundaries that are difficult to distinguish in the dim RGB. In frame 1, the table fills most of the view at roughly 0.5–1.2 m, with a bowl high-centre, utensils left-centre, and a person mask occupying the near right foreground; in frame 2, a cup appears near the upper-left edge, and in frame 3 a seated person is left of centre with the table behind and to the right. Frame 4 isolates a person near the centre at about 0.7–1.3 m, while frame 5 shows two overlapping people across the centre and right, one partly cut off by the right edge; their masks suggest close spacing, roughly within 0–0.6 m of each other, but do not reliably show which person is in front. Missing masks, abrupt class changes, large black gaps, merged table regions, and inconsistent person coverage make facing direction, gaze, occlusion order, and motion across frames unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only two magenta hand skeletons in frame 4: one left of centre and slightly higher, and one right of centre and slightly lower, separated horizontally by roughly 0.4–0.8 m in the scene. Against the RGB, both hands appear in front of seated people and above the tabletop, approximately 0.5–1.2 m from the camera wearer and plausibly within those people's arm reach; neither is clearly within the camera wearer's immediate reach. Their finger orientation provides limited local hand direction, but no body skeletons, heads, or eye landmarks are visible, so facing direction, gaze toward the camera, and person-to-hand assignment cannot be established. The complete absence of poses in frames 1–3 and 5, despite visible people and arms, shows that this map is highly incomplete and cannot reliably support approach, retreat, turning, or occlusion tracking across the sequence.
